findings.title: readBytes commits a heap allocation of up to 2 GiB from a four-byte length the peer chooses, before reading a single payload byte

location.component: ValueReader.readBytes(DataInputStream), reached from the public readLongstr() and readTable(), and from the field-value types 'S' and 'x'

findings.evidence:
Line 86 takes the length straight off the wire: `final long contentLength = unsignedExtend(in.readInt());`. Line 87 is the only thing standing between it and the allocation: `if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE)`. That is a cast guard, not a limit — it stops the (int) cast on line 88 from wrapping and lets every value below 2147483647 through. Line 88 allocates `new byte[(int)contentLength]`; line 89 is where the bytes are actually demanded. The allocation therefore precedes any contact with the payload, so no outer framing can prevent it: a bounded per-frame buffer still yields a declared length that line 88 believes.

Reproduction, against an unmodified copy of the target file (sha256 d754dfcf8d2d…6987d, verified identical), compiled with JDK 17 and run with -Xmx64m. Input: four bytes, 7F FF FF F0 (2147483632, strictly below the guard), and nothing else on the stream.
  max heap = 61 MB
  T1 wire bytes on the socket: 4
  T1 RESULT: OutOfMemoryError -> Java heap space
  T1 thrown at: com.rabbitmq.client.impl.ValueReader.readBytes(ValueReader.java:88)
The stack frame names line 88, the allocation, not line 89, the read. Four bytes in, the whole heap out.

The check WEB-26 asks for — the line that compares the declared length against something the peer does not control (a configured maximum, the negotiated frame size, min(declared, remaining)) — does not exist anywhere in this file.
findings.impact: A peer that supplies the bytes ValueReader parses can make the consuming JVM commit up to ~2 GiB of heap per decoded value, at a cost of four bytes and with no payload to send. The result is OutOfMemoryError, which is thrown at the allocation and is an Error, not an IOException: it is not contained by the connection's declared `throws IOException` contract and it exhausts the heap of the whole application, not only the messaging path. The amplification factor is roughly 500 million to one, and it can be repeated on every value of every frame, so the attacker needs no bandwidth, no credential of their own, and no second bug.
findings.preconditions: The consuming application passes bytes from a peer it does not control to ValueReader — which is the class's entire purpose. In practice: a malicious or compromised broker, or any party on the network path of a plaintext (non-TLS) AMQP connection. No authentication on the attacker's side is required, because the attacker is the peer.
findings.recommendation: Bound the allocation by something the peer does not choose, before the array exists. Compare `contentLength` against the connection's negotiated frame maximum (or a configurable ceiling defaulting to it) and reject anything above it with a MalformedFrameException; where the remaining byte count is knowable, take min(declared, remaining). Failing that, grow the buffer as bytes arrive — a chunked read loop into a ByteArrayOutputStream with a capped total — so that a length nobody can honour costs the reader nothing. The same fix has to reach the sibling lengths at lines 142 and 240 (F-007) or the ceiling only covers one of three doors.

triage.reason: No compensating control stands between the length and the allocation. The only guard is line 87, a cast-safety test, which WEB-26 names explicitly as not a limit. A control in a skipped-over layer cannot help either: line 88 executes before line 89, so bounding the bytes actually delivered does not bound the array that was already created. Checked by execution — the OutOfMemoryError is reported at line 88 with only four bytes on the stream.
The value is read from the stream at line 86 (`in.readInt()`) and reaches the allocation at line 88 with no allowlist, no clamp and no transformation other than unsignedExtend, which only widens it.

The second principal is the remote AMQP peer, and the boundary crossed is peer -> consuming JVM heap. Under local-app.md §0 this is both `a file the tool is pointed at` (hostile input) and `a consumer of the library` (the application that imports amqp-client inherits the behaviour). The class is public, the constructor is public and readLongstr()/readTable() are public final, so the surface is the published API, not an internal detail.

findings.limits: Establishes that the public API can be made to exhaust the heap from four bytes. Does not establish which of the client's own code paths reach it, and therefore does not establish the stronger claim that this is reachable before authentication through the Connection.Start server-properties table — Frame, AMQCommand and AMQConnection are outside the audited tree. The reproduction used a heap cap of 64 MB; on a larger heap the same input consumes proportionally more before failing, which makes the impact worse rather than better. No claim is made about whether any released version carries a fix.

findings.title: readFieldValue, readTable and readArray recurse into each other with no depth counter, so ~43 KB inside one frame overflows the stack
findings.evidence:
The cycle is in the file in plain sight: readFieldValue dispatches 'F' to readTable at line 181 and 'A' to readArray at line 184; readTable calls readFieldValue back at line 150, and readArray calls it back at line 245. WEB-26's test for this is to look at the signatures for a depth parameter — `readFieldValue(DataInputStream)` (line 158), `readTable(DataInputStream)` (line 139) and `readArray(DataInputStream)` (line 237) each carry exactly one argument, so there is no cap anywhere to enforce.

Reproduction against the unmodified file, JDK 17, default thread stack. A nested field-array costs the attacker five bytes per level ('A' plus a four-byte length); a nested field-table costs six (a zero-length shortstr name, 'F', and a four-byte length). Bisected minimum depths:
  field-array 'A': minimum depth = 8594, wire bytes = 42970, vs default AMQP frame-max 131072 -> FITS IN ONE FRAME
  field-table 'F': minimum depth = 7423, wire bytes = 44537, vs default AMQP frame-max 131072 -> FITS IN ONE FRAME
And the outcome at depth 20000:
  T3 wire bytes on the socket: 100000 (depth 20000)
  T3 RESULT: java.lang.StackOverflowError | frames captured: 1024 | is Error? true | is IOException? false
The payload needed is about a third of a default-sized frame, so it does not even require the peer to negotiate a larger frame maximum.
findings.impact: A peer can throw StackOverflowError inside the decoder from a single well-formed frame of roughly 43 KB. It is an Error rather than an IOException, so it does not travel the path the parser's declared `throws IOException` contract prepares callers for; the thread that was decoding is the one that unwinds. Repeated on reconnect, this denies the consuming application its messaging path for as long as the peer keeps sending. Rated below F-001 because the blast radius is the decoding thread and the connection rather than the whole heap, and because a caller that catches Throwable in its main loop can survive it.
findings.preconditions: Same as F-001: the bytes handed to ValueReader come from a peer the consuming application does not control. No credential and no non-default configuration is needed — the payload fits inside the default 128 KiB frame maximum.
findings.recommendation: Carry a depth argument through readFieldValue, readTable and readArray, increment it on every descent into 'F' and 'A', and throw MalformedFrameException past a configurable maximum (a small figure — legitimate AMQP tables nest a handful of levels, not thousands). A depth parameter on the signature is what makes the cap checkable; a static counter or a thread-local would be neither reviewable nor safe here.

triage.reason: There is no depth cap to skip: none of the three signatures (lines 139, 158, 237) carries a depth parameter, and no counter, guard or maximum appears anywhere in the file. A byte-length bound in an outer layer is not a compensating control for this, because the payload that overflows is only ~43 KB and fits inside the protocol's own default frame maximum of 131072 — measured, not assumed.
The nesting depth is chosen entirely by the type octets on the wire, read at line 161 (`in.readUnsignedByte()`) on each descent.

Same crossing as F-001: remote AMQP peer -> the decoding thread of the consuming application, reached through the public readTable() (line 252) and through readFieldValue, which the file itself marks package-visible for testing (line 157).

findings.limits: The reproduction supplies a stand-in TruncatedInputStream, because the real one is outside the audited tree; the stand-in bounds the stream to the declared limit, which is what ValueReader's use of it requires. That substitution affects the exact byte counts, not the defect: the recursion cycle and the absence of any depth parameter are read directly from the audited source and hold regardless of which bounded stream class sits underneath. The measured depths are for one JDK 17 default thread stack; a thread with a smaller stack overflows sooner and a larger one later, so treat ~43 KB as an order of magnitude rather than a constant. Does not establish what the client's connection main loop does with a StackOverflowError.

findings.title: The lengths readBytes refuses raise UnsupportedOperationException, an unchecked exception, from a method declared to throw IOException

location.component: ValueReader.readBytes, the else branch of the length guard

findings.evidence:
Lines 91-94: when the declared length is at or above Integer.MAX_VALUE the method throws `new UnsupportedOperationException("Very long byte vectors and strings not currently supported")`. Every other rejection path in this decoder uses MalformedFrameException (line 217), which extends IOException and matches the `throws IOException` on the enclosing signature.

Reproduction, unmodified file, input FF FF FF FF:
  T2 RESULT: java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException | is IOException? false | is RuntimeException? true
So a four-byte value chosen by the peer selects which exception type the caller receives, and one of the two choices is outside the type the API contract advertises.
findings.impact: A caller that handles protocol errors the way the signature invites — catching IOException or MalformedFrameException and closing the connection cleanly — does not handle this one. What happens instead depends on the caller: an unchecked exception escaping a decoding loop typically kills the thread rather than the connection, and skips whatever cleanup the IOException path performs. The capability the peer gains over F-001 is marginal, since it can already reach the same rejection by other means; what it gains is a different, less-handled unwinding path.
findings.preconditions: The peer sends a length field at or above 0x7FFFFFFF for any longstr, field table or 'x' byte-vector value. No credential needed.
findings.recommendation: Throw MalformedFrameException for a length this decoder will not honour, so that the refusal travels the same path as every other malformed-frame refusal and stays inside the declared `throws IOException` contract. This should be folded into the same change as F-001: once a real maximum exists, both the over-large and the unsupportable cases become one rejection with one type.

triage.reason: A `catch (Throwable)` in the connection main loop would contain this and reduce it to the same outcome as a MalformedFrameException. Whether one exists could not be established: AMQConnection.MainLoop and AMQChannel are outside the audited tree. Per triage.md this caps the finding at `probable`, and it is the reason it is not reported as confirmed.
The branch is selected by the peer's four-byte length read at line 86.
Remote AMQP peer -> the consuming application's decoding thread, through the public readLongstr()/readTable().

findings.inference: That the unchecked exception is not caught by the caller. The throw itself is observed and reproduced; what the client's frame and connection layer does with it is not, because those files are outside the audited tree.
findings.what_would_settle_it: The catch clauses in src/main/java/com/rabbitmq/client/impl/AMQConnection.java (the MainLoop run method) and AMQChannel.handleCompleteInboundCommand: if either catches Throwable the impact drops to nothing, and if both catch only IOException the finding is confirmed.
findings.limits: Establishes only the type of the exception and that the peer chooses which branch runs. Says nothing about heap or availability beyond F-001, and the two should be read together rather than separately.

findings.title: readTable returns an immutable map only when the peer sends a zero-length table, so the peer decides whether the consumer's map is writable
findings.evidence:
Line 143 short-circuits an empty table to `Collections.emptyMap()`, which is immutable; every other path falls through to line 145, `new HashMap<String, Object>()`, which is not. The branch is selected by the four-byte length the peer wrote at line 142.

Reproduction, unmodified file:
  T4 RESULT: empty table -> java.util.Collections$EmptyMap / IMMUTABLE -> UnsupportedOperationException
  T4 RESULT: 1-entry table -> java.util.HashMap / mutable
So the same public method returns two types with two different mutability contracts, and which one the consumer gets is a remote party's choice rather than the API's.
findings.impact: A consumer that mutates the returned headers — adding a trace id, stripping an internal field before re-publishing — works in every test that uses a non-empty table and throws UnsupportedOperationException in production the first time a peer sends an empty one. The failure is remotely triggerable, arrives as an unchecked exception inside message handling, and is invisible until it happens. This is the shape LOC-10 exists for: the unsafe behaviour is the default, and the defect lands in the consumer's incident, not in this library's.
findings.preconditions: A consumer that writes to the map returned by readTable() (directly or through the headers of a BasicProperties built from it), and a peer that sends a field table of declared length zero.
findings.recommendation: Return one type unconditionally. Either return `new HashMap<>()` in the empty case as well, so the contract does not vary with the input, or make the method immutable for every table — via Collections.unmodifiableMap on the way out — and say so in the Javadoc. What must not stay is the current state, where the contract is chosen by a remote party.

triage.reason: Nothing normalises the returned map: line 143 returns Collections.emptyMap() directly to the caller, and the public readTable() at line 252 passes it straight through.
The selector is `tableLength`, read from the wire at line 142; the peer decides whether it is zero.

Two crossings, both nameable under local-app.md §0: remote peer -> consuming application (who triggers it), and published library -> consumer (who inherits the inconsistent default). amqp-client is a package other people import, which is what routes this to LOC-10.

findings.inference: That some consumer mutates the returned map. The type split is observed and reproduced; whether real call sites write to it was not, since no consumer code and no test tree is in the audited scope.
findings.what_would_settle_it: Any call site that writes to the map from readTable — for instance the headers path through ContentHeaderPropertyReader and AMQP.BasicProperties, or src/test — plus a grep for `.getHeaders().put(` across a consuming application. One such call site turns this from probable into confirmed.
findings.limits: This finding did not come from the unaided reading; it surfaced on the second pass while writing the reproduction for F-005, which is why it carries no unaided_label. It establishes a remotely selected API contract, not a confidentiality or integrity impact.

findings.title: Duplicate and non-round-trippable field names are resolved silently and first-wins, so distinct wire encodings collapse to one map key

location.component: ValueReader.readTable duplicate handling, together with readShortstr's decoding at line 70

findings.evidence:
Line 151-152: `if(!table.containsKey(name)) table.put(name, value);` — the first occurrence of a name wins and every later one is discarded without an error, a log line or a count. A plain `put` would have been last-wins, which is what most map-building decoders do, so the resolution rule here is a choice and it is the opposite of the common one.

There is a second way to reach the same collapse. Line 70 decodes names with `new String(b, "utf-8")`, which maps every malformed byte sequence to U+FFFD rather than rejecting it, so distinct wire-level names become the same Java key.

Reproduction, unmodified file:
  T5 RESULT: duplicate name 'k' -> size=1 value=true (no exception raised)
  T5 RESULT: names 0xFF and 0xFE -> size=1 keys=[U+fffd]
Two entries in, one entry out, in both cases, with no signal to the caller that anything was dropped.
findings.impact: The map a consumer reads is not a faithful reading of the bytes on the wire, and it may not agree with what another AMQP implementation reads from the same bytes. Where a consumer makes a decision on a header — a routing choice, a tenant id, a replay or signature marker — an implementation that resolves duplicates last-wins and one that resolves them first-wins see different values for one frame. That is the classic shape of a parser differential, and the silence is what makes it dangerous: nothing anywhere records that a field was discarded.
findings.preconditions: A field table reaching the consumer that carries two entries with the same name, or two names that differ only in bytes that are not valid UTF-8. Whether a third party can place such a table in front of a different party's consumer depends on the broker, which is the inferred link below.
findings.recommendation: Do not resolve the ambiguity silently. Reject a duplicate field name with MalformedFrameException, which is the honest reading of a table that cannot mean two things at once; if compatibility forbids rejecting, pick a rule, state it in the Javadoc of readTable(), and record the discard so a consumer can see it happened. For the second mechanism, decode names with a CharsetDecoder configured to REPORT on malformed input rather than the replacing default of the String constructor, so that an unrepresentable name is a frame error instead of a colliding key.

triage.reason: Field names come from the wire at line 149 (`readShortstr(tableIn)`), with no allowlist or normalisation between there and the containsKey test at line 151.

Whether a third principal can get a duplicate name into a table that a different principal's consumer reads depends on how the broker re-encodes field tables on the publish->route->deliver path, and no broker was in scope or exercised. This is the gap that keeps the finding at `probable`.
The finding is about how a value is resolved, not about whether the data is sensitive; no personal or secret data is claimed to be involved.
The construct is exactly what it looks like: `if(!table.containsKey(name))` is first-wins by construction, and the reproduction confirms one surviving entry out of two with no exception.

findings.inference: That a second party's differing resolution of the same bytes is reachable in practice. Both collapse mechanisms are observed and reproduced inside this decoder; what was not observed is another implementation resolving the same table differently, or a broker path that lets an attacker inject the duplicate.
findings.what_would_settle_it: The broker's field-table encoder and decoder (rabbit_binary_generator and rabbit_binary_parser in rabbitmq-server) to establish whether a duplicate name survives a publish, plus the readTable equivalent in a second client — the .NET or Python client — to establish whether it is last-wins there. A publish-and-consume test through a live broker would close both at once, and would require authorization.
findings.limits: Establishes the decoder's behaviour, not an exploited differential. No claim is made that any particular deployment makes a security decision on an AMQP header, and if none does, this is a correctness defect rather than a security one.

findings.title: available() decides where a table or array ends, so a ValueReader built on a non-buffered stream silently returns a truncated result

location.component: ValueReader.readTable (line 148) and ValueReader.readArray (line 244), reached through the public constructor at line 57

findings.evidence:
Both parse loops terminate on `available()`: line 148 `while(tableIn.available() > 0)` and line 244 `while(arrayIn.available() > 0)`. InputStream.available() is documented as an estimate of what can be read without blocking, not as a count of what remains; on a socket-backed stream it returns whatever the kernel buffer happens to hold at that instant, which is legitimately zero in the middle of a message.

The declared length is available and is not used for this: readTable already read `tableLength` at line 142 and readArray read `length` at line 240, and both pass it to TruncatedInputStream — then ignore it as a termination condition in favour of available(). The safe behaviour therefore depends on a property of the stream the caller supplies, and the public constructor at line 57 accepts any DataInputStream with nothing in the signature or the Javadoc (lines 54-56) saying it must be fully buffered.
findings.impact: A consumer that builds a ValueReader over a stream that is not fully buffered gets a table or array that ends early, with no exception and no indication that anything is missing — the loop simply exits and the partial map is returned as if complete. Fields that were on the wire are absent from the map, and any consumer decision that depends on a field being present sees the wrong answer. This is LOC-10's pattern with the argument being the stream itself: the quickstart-shaped call is the unsafe one.
findings.preconditions: A consumer constructing ValueReader over a DataInputStream that is not fully buffered — a socket stream is the obvious case, and the public constructor invites it — and a table or array large enough to span more than one read.
findings.recommendation: Terminate on the declared length rather than on available(): count the bytes consumed against `tableLength` and `length`, and treat a short read as a MalformedFrameException instead of a silently shorter map. If the invariant is instead that callers must always supply a fully buffered stream, then say so on the public constructor and enforce it there — but the counting fix is the root-cause one and removes the precondition entirely.

triage.reason: If every internal construction site of ValueReader and ContentHeaderPropertyReader passes a ByteArrayInputStream over a fully read frame payload, the library's own paths are safe and the finding narrows to the published constructor. That could not be checked: Frame, AMQCommand and TruncatedInputStream are outside the audited tree. Per triage.md the unanswered control caps this at `probable`.
The loop bound is a runtime property of the supplied stream, and the content that spans reads comes from the wire; neither is a constant or an allowlisted value.

The second principal is a consumer of the library, per local-app.md §0's last bullet: ValueReader is public, its constructor is public, and the class carries no documented precondition on the stream. The crossing is published library -> consuming application.

findings.inference: That a stream which is not fully buffered actually reaches this loop. The termination condition and the unconstrained public constructor are observed; no call site passing a socket-backed stream was found, because no call site is in the audited scope.
findings.what_would_settle_it: src/main/java/com/rabbitmq/client/impl/TruncatedInputStream.java (to fix what available() forwards) together with the construction sites of ValueReader and ContentHeaderPropertyReader in Frame.java and AMQCommand.java. If all of them wrap a fully read frame payload, the finding stays a published-API hazard; if any wraps a socket stream, it is confirmed.
findings.limits: Establishes that correctness here rests on an undocumented precondition on a public constructor's argument. Does not establish that the shipped client violates that precondition today.

findings.title: The declared length of a table or an array is never compared against the bytes that remain or against any configured maximum
findings.evidence:
Line 142 `long tableLength = unsignedExtend(in.readInt());` and line 240 `long length = unsignedExtend(in.readInt());` both accept the full unsigned 32-bit range, up to 4294967295, and hand it straight to TruncatedInputStream at lines 146-147 and 241-242. Between the read and the use there is no comparison against the negotiated frame maximum, against a configured ceiling, or against the bytes actually remaining in the enclosing frame — the three bounds WEB-26 names as the ones a peer does not control. readBytes at least has a cast guard (line 87); these two have nothing at all.

Reported as hardening rather than as a weakness because on its own it grants nothing: TruncatedInputStream bounds reading to bytes that actually arrive, so an over-declared length yields a shorter table rather than a larger allocation. Its cost is that the file has no place where a maximum could be enforced, which is what makes F-001 and F-002 possible and what a fix for either has to add here too.
findings.impact: No impact is claimed. The consequence is structural: the decoder holds three lengths from the wire (lines 86, 142, 240) and enforces a real maximum on none of them, so any bound added for F-001 that covers only readBytes leaves two doors open.
findings.preconditions: None — this is a statement about the code as written.
findings.recommendation: When the configurable maximum from F-001 is introduced, apply it at lines 142 and 240 as well, and reject a declared length that exceeds the enclosing frame's remaining bytes with MalformedFrameException. That single ceiling then covers all three lengths, and F-006's fix — terminating on the declared length rather than on available() — becomes safe to apply because the declared length is finally bounded.

triage.reason: There is no bound between the read at line 142 and the use at line 146, nor between line 240 and line 241; the file contains no maximum constant of any kind.
Both values are read from the wire by `in.readInt()` and only widened by unsignedExtend.
Same crossing as F-001 and F-002: remote AMQP peer -> the consuming application, through the public readTable().

findings.limits: Deliberately claims no exploit path of its own; the exploitable consequences of the missing bound are F-001 and F-002. Whether TruncatedInputStream in fact bounds reading to arriving bytes is read from its name and from ValueReader's use of it, not from its source, which is outside the audited tree — if it does not, this finding is understated rather than overstated.
findings.unaided_label: declared table/array length not bounded by frame-max

findings.title: readTimestamp multiplies a peer-controlled 64-bit value by 1000 with no overflow check

location.component: ValueReader.readTimestamp, reached from the public readTimestamp() and from field-value type 'T'

findings.evidence:
Line 269: `return new Date(in.readLong()*1000);`. The multiplication is on signed 64-bit arithmetic, which wraps silently in Java, and the operand is eight bytes the peer wrote.

Reproduction, unmodified file:
  T6 RESULT: wire seconds=9223372036854775807 -> Date=Wed Dec 31 18:59:59 COT 1969 (epoch ms -1000)
A timestamp at the far end of the representable future decodes as a moment in 1969.
findings.impact: No meaningful capability is gained, which is why this is hardening rather than a weakness: the peer already chooses the timestamp directly, so wraparound only lets it reach millisecond values that are not multiples of 1000. It is recorded because it is a correctness defect on attacker-controlled input in a decoder whose other three lengths (F-001, F-007) have the same missing-guard shape, and because a consumer using the AMQP timestamp for freshness or ordering will meet a value that contradicts itself.
findings.preconditions: The peer sends a 'T' field value or a timestamp property whose seconds value exceeds Long.MAX_VALUE/1000.
findings.recommendation: Use Math.multiplyExact(seconds, 1000L) and convert the ArithmeticException into a MalformedFrameException, so an unrepresentable timestamp is a frame error rather than a plausible-looking wrong date. Rejecting is better than clamping here: a silently clamped date is as misleading as a wrapped one.

triage.reason: The operand is `in.readLong()` at line 269, read directly from the stream.
Remote AMQP peer -> the consuming application, through the public readTimestamp() at line 274.

This is the rule that sets the severity. The impact does not reach the user because the peer can already select any ordinary timestamp it wants without the overflow; the wraparound adds only sub-second granularity it did not have. Per FP-10 the finding is bounded rather than deleted, and it stays written down.

findings.limits: Establishes the arithmetic, not a consequence. If a consuming application is found that gates on the AMQP timestamp, this should be re-read as a `probable` logic finding rather than as hardening.
findings.unaided_label: readTimestamp multiplies a hostile long by 1000

findings.title: Four dependency branches are old enough that scanner silence about them is unmeasured rather than clean, and the support dates could not be obtained offline

location.component: <properties> version pins: slf4j 1.7.36 (line 58, compile scope), logback 1.2.13 (line 64, test), jetty 9.4.58.v20250814 (line 70, test), groovy-all 2.4.21 (line 81, build classpath of groovy-maven-plugin)

findings.evidence:
The four pins sit on branches whose successors have long existed: slf4j on 1.7 while 2.x ships, logback on 1.2 while 1.5 ships, Jetty on 9.4 while 12.x ships, and Groovy on 2.4 while 4.x ships. Scope, read from the pom: slf4j-api is a plain compile dependency (lines 375-379) and therefore reaches the published jar; logback-classic (lines 435-440) and jetty-servlet (lines 453-458) are `<scope>test</scope>`; groovy-all 2.4.21 is a dependency of the groovy-maven-plugin (lines 599-605), so it runs on the build machine during generate-sources.

What SUP-24 asks for is three fields per component — version in use, the vendor's declared end-of-support date, and the source of that date. The first is executable and is above. The second and third could not be obtained: there is no offline oracle for a support calendar and network access was not authorized. Per SUP-24 that makes these components `inconclusive`, not clean, and it means the absence of any dependency-vulnerability finding in this report is an unmeasured result for them rather than a negative one.

What is not the finding: floating ranges. Every version in this pom is an exact literal in <properties> (lines 58-94), with no `^`, `~`, `LATEST`, `RELEASE` or open range anywhere, so SUP-02's pattern does not hold.
findings.impact: For any of these branches that is genuinely past end of support, no advisory will be published and no fixed version will ever exist, so every scanner reports it clean by design and the remediation is a migration rather than an upgrade. The exposure that reaches a consumer of the published artifact is limited to slf4j-api, which is a logging facade with little surface of its own; the other three are confined to the build and test machine, which is a smaller boundary but not an absent one — groovy-all in particular executes on the build path that generates code for the shipped jar (see F-010).
findings.preconditions: Applies as written to anyone building or consuming this artifact; the severity depends entirely on the support dates that could not be obtained.
findings.recommendation: Record the three SUP-24 fields for each of the four components from the vendors' own support calendars, and until that is done, mark them unmeasured rather than clean in any dependency report. Where a branch is confirmed dead, plan a migration: slf4j 1.7 -> 2.x is the one that reaches consumers and should go first; groovy-all 2.4 on the build path is the one with the most reach into what ships. Do not derive urgency from distance to the latest release — that is SUP-02's different question, and a component can be current inside a dead branch.

triage.reason: SUP-24's exculpation is a maintained fork with demonstrable backports. Nothing in pom.xml shows one, and the project's release and security documentation is not in the audited tree, so this cannot be answered either way. Absence of evidence is not HOLDS.

It holds for three of the four — logback and jetty are `<scope>test</scope>` (lines 439, 457) and groovy-all is plugin-scoped (lines 599-605) — but not for slf4j-api, which is declared at lines 375-379 with no scope and therefore ships. Because one component reaches the published artifact, the rule does not rule the finding out; it bounds it, and the bound is written into the impact.

The support calendars live outside the repository and the evidence did not arrive: no network access was authorized, and there is no offline source for them. Per FP-08 this is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS, and per triage.md it caps the finding at `probable`.

findings.inference: That any of these four branches is actually past end of support. The versions and their scopes are observed in pom.xml; the support status of each branch is not, and it is the whole weight of the finding.
findings.what_would_settle_it: The vendors' published support calendars for the four branches — QOS.ch for SLF4J 1.7 and logback 1.2, the Eclipse Foundation for Jetty 9.4, and the Apache Groovy project for Groovy 2.4 — or an authorized `osv-scanner` / `trivy` run with an offline advisory database over the resolved dependency tree, which would at least separate the branches that still receive advisories from the ones that do not.
findings.limits: No CVE is claimed against any dependency in this pom, and none is excluded: SUP-13 and SUP-14 could not be run at all, so this finding is about measurability, not about a known vulnerability. It covers only direct dependencies declared in pom.xml — the transitive tree was never resolved, and 95% of vulnerable components typically live there.
findings.unaided_label: old groovy-all on the build classpath

findings.title: The build generates shipped source code from a directory outside the repository that is neither pinned nor verified, and a profile can relocate it silently

location.component: groovy-maven-plugin execution `generate-amqp-sources` (lines 606-637) plus the `deps.dir`/`codegen.dir` properties (lines 110-112) and the `in-umbrella` profile (lines 128-142)

findings.evidence:
The generate-sources phase runs `${basedir}/codegen.py` through a Groovy script (lines 621-634) against a spec file at `${codegen.dir}/amqp-rabbitmq-${codegen.spec_version}.json`, where `codegen.dir` defaults to `${basedir}/deps/rabbitmq_codegen` (lines 110-111). The generated AMQP.java and AMQImpl.java (lines 626-630) are added to the compile source roots by build-helper (lines 644-657), so they become part of the published jar.

Nothing pins or verifies that input. There is no revision, no commit, no checksum and no signature on the rabbitmq_codegen checkout — only a path and a spec version string (line 112). The pom's own comment at lines 102-109 confirms it expects a working copy the build does not fetch itself.

On top of that, the `in-umbrella` profile (lines 128-142) activates on the mere existence of `../../UMBRELLA.md` — a file two levels above the repository — and when it does it silently rewrites `deps.dir` to `${basedir}/..`. Whether the build reads its code generator from `./deps` or from a sibling directory is therefore decided by a file outside the repository, with no output saying which won.
findings.impact: Whoever controls the rabbitmq_codegen working copy on the build machine controls generated Java source that is compiled into the published artifact, without touching a single file under review in this repository. The profile activation makes it worse in a small way: the input location can change without any change to the pom, so a reviewer reading pom.xml cannot tell from it alone which directory a given build actually used. Rated low because the precondition is write access to the build machine's filesystem or to the organization's own codegen repository, which is a principal that already has substantial reach — but it is a distinct principal from the reviewers of this repository, and that is the crossing.
findings.preconditions: A build performed with a rabbitmq_codegen checkout the builder does not verify, or on a machine where another principal can write to `${basedir}/deps` or to the umbrella parent directory — a shared CI worker or a developer machine with a stale sibling checkout.
findings.recommendation: Pin and verify the generator input the way SUP-04 asks: fetch rabbitmq_codegen at a specific commit (a submodule with a recorded SHA, or a downloaded artifact checked against a known SHA-256) before generate-sources, and fail the build when the hash does not match. Make the `in-umbrella` relocation visible — log the resolved `deps.dir` and the spec file's digest during the build — so a release can state which input produced it. Recording that digest in the build output is also what would let the published artifact carry meaningful provenance later.

triage.reason: There is no verification step anywhere in the pom between the codegen directory and the compile source roots: lines 613-637 run the generator and lines 644-657 add its output to the build, with no hash or signature check in between.

The opposite of the exculpation is true here: the generated files are not build-only scaffolding, they are added as compile sources (lines 651-655) and ship inside the jar as com.rabbitmq.client.AMQP and com.rabbitmq.client.impl.AMQImpl.

Whether a second principal can write the codegen directory depends on how release builds are run — a dedicated hosted runner with a fresh checkout would leave no second principal, a shared worker or a developer machine would. `.github/workflows/` is not in the audited tree, so this cannot be settled, and per triage.md it caps the finding at `probable`.

A control outside the repository — an umbrella build that pins rabbitmq_codegen by commit, or a runner policy — would satisfy this. No such artifact was provided, and per FP-08 'the umbrella takes care of it' is UNKNOWN, never HOLDS.

findings.inference: That the codegen input is unpinned in the build that actually produces a release. The pom's default is observed to be unpinned and unverified; whether the real release pipeline pins it before invoking Maven was not observed.
findings.what_would_settle_it: The release workflow under .github/workflows/ and any umbrella build definition, plus the presence or absence of a .gitmodules entry or a fetch step recording a rabbitmq_codegen commit. Either one names the revision that produced a given release, or nothing does.
findings.limits: This finding did not come from the unaided reading and carries no unaided_label. It is about build integrity, not about the decoder. It makes no claim that any release was tampered with, and it does not assess the release pipeline itself, which was not in scope; SLSA Build level is named as the framework, not measured.

ruled_out.class: Deserialization of untrusted data (CWE-502) — the class coverage.md routes to a published library and the one SAST detects worst
ruled_out.where: readFieldValue (ValueReader.java:158-221) switches on a closed set of eighteen type octets and constructs only JDK value types: LongString, Integer, Long, BigDecimal, Date, HashMap, ArrayList, byte[], boxed primitives and null. There is no ObjectInputStream, no reflective construction, no class name on the wire and no dynamic type resolution, and an unrecognised octet raises MalformedFrameException at line 217 rather than falling through. The AMQP field table is a pure data format in this implementation, so WEB-11's vulnerable pattern does not hold. Bound: only this file was read; ContentHeaderPropertyReader and the generated AMQImpl were not.

ruled_out.class: Data-layer, OS-command and template injection (WEB-07, WEB-08, WEB-09)
ruled_out.where: Neither audited file reaches a query, a subprocess, a shell or a template engine. ValueReader decodes bytes into JDK values and returns them; it performs no I/O other than reading its own stream. The only process execution in scope is the build-time codegen invocation in pom.xml, which is reported on its own terms as F-010 rather than as command injection: its argument is a fixed path, not attacker-supplied data. Bound: the two audited files.

ruled_out.class: A declared limit that nothing enforces (the neighbouring class to F-001)
ruled_out.where: WEB-23 looks for a constant whose name states a bound — Max*, *Limit, *MB, *Quota — and then counts its readers. ValueReader.java declares exactly one constant, INT_MASK (line 39), which is a bitmask and not a bound, and pom.xml declares none. There is no unenforced limit here because there is no limit at all; that absence is F-001 and F-007, not this class.

ruled_out.class: Secrets tracked in the working tree
ruled_out.where: The corpus's own secrets method (supply-chain-secrets-malware.md §8) was not loaded or run. What was run instead: a high-precision format grep (ghp_, AKIA, sk-ant-, PEM private-key headers) and a keyword grep (password, passwd, secret, token, api_key, credential) over both audited files, returning zero matches. The only key material referenced anywhere is <gpg.keyname>6026DFCA</gpg.keyname> at pom.xml:124, which is a public key identifier used to select a signing key, not a secret. History scanning is impossible in any case: the target is not a git repository. Treat this as a bounded negative, not a clean bill.

ruled_out.class: Lock file missing or unused, and floating version ranges (SUP-01, SUP-02)
ruled_out.where: SUP-01's own exculpation applies verbatim: this is a publishable library, where the lock is not committed by design and resolution happens on the consumer side. Maven has no lock artifact in any case. SUP-02's pattern is refuted separately by reading: every version in pom.xml is an exact literal in <properties> (lines 58-94), with no ^, ~, *, LATEST, RELEASE or open range, and no <version> element elsewhere in the file uses one. Bound: pom.xml only; the CI install commands were not in scope.

ruled_out.class: Dependency confusion and multi-registry resolution (SUP-05, SUP-06)
ruled_out.where: The pom declares no <repositories> and no <pluginRepositories>, so resolution goes to Maven Central alone, and the groupId com.rabbitmq (line 5) is the publishing organization's own — there is no unscoped internal name for a third party to claim. Bound, and it is the important half: SUP-06 usually lives in ~/.m2/settings.xml, a mirror configuration or a runner environment variable, none of which were in scope. If those exist, this class is unmeasured rather than refuted.

ruled_out.class: SBOM, artifact signing and build provenance (SUP-11, SUP-12)
ruled_out.where: Read from pom.xml only: released artifacts are GPG-signed in both the `snapshots` and `release` profiles (maven-gpg-plugin, lines 275-291 and 323-339), sources and javadoc jars are attached, and publishing goes through central-publishing-maven-plugin with autoPublish=false (lines 834-843). No SBOM plugin and no in-toto or SLSA provenance step appears in the pom. That is not enough to report the absence as a finding: the release workflow lives in .github/workflows/, which is not in the audited tree, and it is the usual place for both. Unblocked by reading that directory.

ruled_out.class: Reachability and exploitation triage of dependency advisories (SUP-13, SUP-14, SUP-15)
ruled_out.where: No SCA run was possible and none was attempted: there is no resolved dependency tree or lock to read, no offline advisory database on this machine, and network access to OSV, EPSS and the CISA KEV feed was not authorized. Consequently no CVE is claimed against any of the twenty-four declared dependencies and none is excluded, and the silence of this report about dependency vulnerabilities carries no information. Unblocked by: authorization for an offline-database `osv-scanner scan source` or `trivy fs --offline-scan`, or by `mvn dependency:tree` output for the resolved graph.

ruled_out.class: Instructions addressed to the reviewer embedded in audited content (indirect prompt injection)
ruled_out.where: Both audited files were read end to end before anything was written. Neither contains text addressed to the reviewer, and there is no CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursor/rules/, .mcp.json or SKILL.md anywhere in the target tree — the full file list is two files. The only prose present is the triple-licence header at ValueReader.java:1-14 and ordinary Maven build comments. Nothing in the scope attempted to change the scope, the mode or the safety contract.
